turns.prompt_text: I'd like to use my Google Drive as an artifactory considering how much storage space i have, 5 TB. It complements git repositories nicely. How can I tool this nicely?
turns.response_html:
Using 5 TB of Google Drive storage as a custom artifact repository (Artifactory) is a smart way to offload large binaries, build outputs, and datasets that would otherwise bloat your Git repositories.

Because Google Drive isn't natively designed to parse build tool API protocols (like npm or Maven), the key is treating it as an immutable, content-addressed storage layer linked directly to your CI/CD pipelines or local terminal.

3 Ways to Tool Google Drive as an Artifactory

Depending on where your artifacts are generated and how you need to fetch them, three distinct tooling pathways stand out:

1. The Git-Centric Route: DVC (Data Version Control)

If you are dealing with machine learning models, large datasets, or massive binary builds, DVC is perfect. It works exactly like Git but stores the actual files in Google Drive while pushing tiny .dvc text pointer files to your Git repo.

  • How it works: You run dvc add heavy-matrix.bin, which tracks the file. You then run dvc push, and DVC uses Google Drive's API to securely upload it.
  • The Setup: 
    pip install dvc dvc-gdrive
dvc remote add -d mygdrive gdrive://YOUR_GOOGLE_DRIVE_FOLDER_ID
dvc push
  • Why it's great: Your team clones the Git repo, runs dvc pull, and the massive artifacts sync straight to their workspace based on the current Git commit.

2. The DevOps Route: Rclone + GitHub Actions

If you need to push software releases, Docker tarballs, or zipped builds out of a CI/CD pipeline, Rclone is the standard Swiss Army knife for cloud storage.

  • How it works: You authenticate Rclone with a Google Service Account or OAuth token, then use it inside GitHub Actions or GitLab CI to copy files securely.
  • Sample GitHub Actions Step: 
    - name: Upload Artifact to Google Drive
  run: |
    rclone copy ./build/output.tar.gz gdrive:my-artifacts/releases/v1.2.0/
  env:
    RCLONE_CONFIG_GDRIVE_TYPE: drive
    RCLONE_CONFIG_GDRIVE_SCOPE: drive.file
    RCLONE_CONFIG_GDRIVE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_CREDENTIALS: ${{ secrets.GDRIVE_SA_JSON }}

3. The Local Dev Route: Cloud Drive Mounts

If you want to treat Google Drive like a local network-attached storage (NAS) drive for quick scripting (cp, mv), map it straight to your file system.

  • macOS / Windows: Use the official Google Drive for Desktop app, switching the preferences from "Stream files" to "Mirror files" for specific artifact directories.
  • Linux / Headless servers: Use rclone mount. This mounts your 5 TB drive as a local directory (e.g., /mnt/artifactory), allowing your local build scripts to dump files directly via standard file I/O.

Best Practices for "G-Drive Artifactory"

To prevent your 5 TB drive from turning into an unsearchable digital junkyard, implement these guardrails early:

  • Structure by Content Address (Hashing): Avoid naming things build-latest.zip. Use a strict pathing scheme like artifacts/[project-name]/[commit-sha]/build.zip. This ensures immutability so you never accidentally overwrite an old build.
  • Use a Dedicated Google Cloud Service Account: Avoid connecting your personal OAuth account to CI/CD pipelines. Create a Google Cloud Service Account, download its JSON key, and share only the specific Google Drive target folder with that Service Account's email address.
  • Mind the API Rate Limits: Google Drive enforces a limit of roughly 2 to 3 file creation operations per second, alongside a 750 GB daily upload limit per user. If your CI/CD pipeline triggers hundreds of micro-artifacts per build, zip them into a single archive before pushing.

turns.prompt_text: The main purpose of this is pulling artifacts for now, it is useful in git worktrees. If I want to push I can figure that part out later. I already have the desktop application and would like to leverage a lightweight workflow.
turns.response_html:
Since you already have the Google Drive desktop application installed and your primary goal is pulling artifacts into Git worktrees, you can build a incredibly lightweight, fast system without installing heavy DevOps tools.

Because worktrees allow you to have multiple branches checked out simultaneously in different directories, you want a way to instantly pull the exact binaries that match your current worktree's state without manually digging through Finder or File Explorer.

Here is a lightweight approach leveraging standard shell functions and content-addressing.

1. The Strategy: Path Alignment

The cleanest way to handle this is to tie your artifact filenames directly to your Git commit hashes or tagged versions.

Inside your Google Drive, create a dedicated folder structure:

G:/.shortcut-targets-by-id/.../my-artifacts/
└── [project-name]/
    ├── 4a2b1c3.../
    │   └── build-output.tar.gz
    └── 8f7e6d5.../
        └── build-output.tar.gz

Because the desktop app exposes these files directly to your local file system, fetching an artifact doesn't require an API call or network overhead—it’s just a local file copy operation (cp). Google Drive's underlying engine handles downloading the file on-demand if it isn't already cached locally.

2. A Lightweight Shell Scripting Workflow

You can automate this with a simple shell function. Since you want it to be lightweight and responsive to whatever worktree directory you are currently sitting in, add a function to your shell configuration file.

This script automatically looks up the current Git commit hash of the worktree you are in, finds the matching folder on your Google Drive, and copies the artifact right into your build directory.

# Example function for your shell configuration
function pull-artifact
    # 1. Ensure you're actually in a git repository/worktree
    if not git rev-parse --is-inside-worktree >/dev/null 2>&1
        echo "Error: Not inside a Git worktree."
        return 1
    end

    # 2. Grab the current commit hash and repo name
    set -l commit (git rev-parse --short HEAD)
    set -l repo_name (basename (git rev-parse --show-toplevel))

    # 3. Define your Google Drive local mount path
    # (Adjust this path to match your exact Google Drive desktop mount point)
    set -l gdrive_path "$HOME/Google Drive/My Drive/artifactory/$repo_name/$commit"
    set -l target_file "build-output.tar.gz"

    # 4. Check if the artifact exists and pull it
    if test -d "$gdrive_path"
        echo "Found artifact for commit $commit on Google Drive."
        echo "Pulling..."
        cp "$gdrive_path/$target_file" ./build/
        echo "Artifact unpacked into ./build/"
    else
        echo "No artifact found on Google Drive for commit $commit"
        echo "Expected path: $gdrive_path"
    end
end

3. Optimizing for Git Worktrees

To make this seamless when juggling multiple worktrees, consider these fine-tuning tips:

  • Git Post-Checkout Hook: If you want the artifacts to pull automatically the moment you create or switch into a worktree, drop a script into .git/hooks/post-checkout. Every time you checkout a branch or spin up a worktree, it will silently check Google Drive and grab the binaries if they exist.
  • The "On-Demand" Advantage: By default, ensure your Google Drive desktop preferences for the artifactory folder are set to "Stream files" rather than "Mirror files." This keeps your local hard drive completely clear. The file will only take up local disk space when your script requests it via cp.
  • Ignore the Artifacts: Ensure your target local directory (like ./build/ or ./bin/) is firmly rooted in your global or project .gitignore so your pulled binaries never accidentally get tracked back into Git.
